paragraphs: Alyosha soon reached Madame Hohlakov’s house, a handsome two-story stone house, one of the finest in our town. Madame Hohlakov spent most of her time in another province, where she had an estate, or in Moscow, where she owned a house. Still, she had a house in our town too, handed down from her ancestors. Her estate in our district was the largest of her three, yet until now she had spent very little time in our province. She ran out to Alyosha in the hall.
“Did you get my letter about the new miracle?” She spoke quickly and nervously.
“Yes.”
“Did you show it to everyone? He gave the son back to his mother!”
“He is dying today,” said Alyosha.

“I’ve heard, I know, oh, how I long to talk to you about all this, to you or to someone. No, to you, to you! And how sorry I am that I can’t see him! The whole town is in an uproar, everyone is in suspense. But now—do you know Katerina Ivanovna is here right now?”
“Ah, that’s lucky,” cried Alyosha. “Then I can see her here. She told me yesterday to be sure to come and see her today.”

“I know, I know everything. I’ve heard exactly what happened yesterday—and the atrocious behavior of that—creature. _C’est tragique_, and if I’d been in her place I don’t know what I would have done. And your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch, what do you think of him?—my goodness! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’m forgetting, just imagine; your brother is in there with her, not that dreadful brother who was so shocking yesterday, but the other one, Ivan Fyodorovitch. He’s sitting with her, talking; they’re having a serious conversation. If you could only imagine what’s going on between them now—it’s awful, I tell you it’s lacerating, it’s like some incredible tale of horror. They’re ruining their lives for no reason anyone can see. They both know it and they revel in it. I’ve been watching for you! I’ve been thirsting for you! It’s too much for me, that’s the worst of it. I’ll tell you all about it soon, but now I must speak of something else, the most important thing—I had completely forgotten what’s most important. Tell me, why has Lise been in hysterics? As soon as she heard you were here, she started having hysterics!”

“_Maman_, it’s you who are hysterical now, not I,” Lise’s voice sang out through a tiny crack in the side door. Her voice sounded as though she wanted to laugh and was doing her utmost to hold it in. Alyosha noticed the crack at once, and no doubt Lise was peeping through it, but he couldn’t see her.

“And no wonder, Lise, no wonder ... your whims will make me hysterical too. But she is so ill, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she has been so ill all night, feverish and moaning! I could hardly wait for morning and for Herzenstube to come. He says he can make nothing of it, that we must wait. Herzenstube always comes and says he can make nothing of it. As soon as you came near the house, she screamed, went into hysterics, and insisted on being wheeled back into this room.”
“Mamma, I didn’t know he had come. It wasn’t because of him that I wanted to be wheeled into this room.”
“That’s not true, Lise. Yulia ran to tell you that Alexey Fyodorovitch was coming. She was on the lookout for you.”

“My darling mamma, that wasn’t at all clever of you. But if you want to make up for it and say something very clever, dear mamma, you’d better tell our honored visitor, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that he has shown how witless he is by daring to come to us after what happened yesterday, when everyone is laughing at him.”

“Lise, you go too far. I swear I shall have to be strict with you. Who is laughing at him? I’m so glad he has come, I need him, I can’t do without him. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I am terribly unhappy!”
“But what’s the matter with you, mamma, darling?”

“Ah, your whims, Lise, your fidgeting, your illness, that awful night of fever, that awful, everlasting Herzenstube, everlasting, everlasting, that’s the worst of it! Everything, in fact, everything.... Even that miracle, too! Oh, how it has upset me, how it has shaken me to pieces, that miracle, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch! And that tragedy in the drawing room, it’s more than I can bear, I warn you. I can’t bear it. A comedy, perhaps, not a tragedy. Tell me, will Father Zossima live till tomorrow, will he? Oh, my God! What is happening to me? Every minute I close my eyes and see that it’s all nonsense, all nonsense.”
“I would be very grateful,” Alyosha interrupted suddenly, “if you could give me a clean rag to bind up my finger. I’ve hurt it, and it hurts a lot.”
Alyosha unwrapped his bitten finger. The handkerchief was soaked with blood. Madame Hohlakov screamed and shut her eyes.
“Good heavens, what a wound, how awful!”
But as soon as Lise saw Alyosha’s finger through the crack, she flung the door wide open.

“Come, come in here,” she cried, imperiously. “No nonsense now! Good heavens, why did you stand there all this time without saying anything about it? He might have bled to death, mamma! How did you do it? Water, water! You must wash it first of all, just hold it in cold water to stop the pain, and keep it there, keep it there.... Hurry, mamma, some water in a slop basin. But do hurry,” she finished nervously. She was thoroughly frightened at the sight of Alyosha’s wound.
“Shouldn’t we send for Herzenstube?” cried Madame Hohlakov.

“Mamma, you’ll be the death of me. Your Herzenstube will come and say he can make nothing of it! Water, water! Mamma, for goodness’ sake go yourself and hurry Yulia, she is such a slowpoke and can never come quickly! Hurry, mamma, or I’ll die.”
“Why, it’s nothing much,” cried Alyosha, frightened by all this alarm.
Yulia ran in with water and Alyosha put his finger in it.

“Some lint, mamma, for mercy’s sake, bring some lint and that muddy lotion for wounds, what’s it called? We’ve got some. You know where the bottle is, mamma; it’s in your bedroom in the right-hand cupboard, there’s a big bottle of it there with the lint.”
“I’ll bring everything in a minute, Lise, only don’t scream and don’t fuss. You see how bravely Alexey Fyodorovitch bears it. Where did you get such a dreadful wound, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Madame Hohlakov hurried away. This was all Lise had been waiting for.
“First of all, answer my question: where did you get hurt like this?” she asked Alyosha, quickly. “And then I’ll talk to you about something quite different. Well?”

Alyosha sensed that the time her mother was away was precious to her. He hurried to tell her about his puzzling meeting with the schoolboys in as few words as he could. Lise clasped her hands as she listened.

“How can you, and in that outfit too, mix with schoolboys?” she cried angrily, as though she had a right to order him about. “You’re nothing but a boy yourself if you can do that, a perfect boy! But you must find out for me about that horrid boy and tell me all about it, because there’s some mystery in it. Now for the second thing, but first a question: does the pain stop you from talking about utterly unimportant things, but talking sensibly?”
“Of course not, and I don’t feel much pain now.”

“That’s because your finger is in the water. The water must be changed right away, because it will get warm in a minute. Yulia, bring some ice from the cellar and another basin of water. Now she’s gone, I can speak; will you give me the letter I sent you yesterday, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch—be quick, because mamma will be back in a minute and I don’t want—”
“I haven’t got the letter.”
“That’s not true, you have. I knew you would say that. You’ve got it in that pocket. I’ve been regretting that joke all night. Give me back the letter at once, give it to me.”
“I left it at home.”

“But you can’t think of me as a child, a little girl, after that silly joke! I’m sorry for that silliness, but you must bring me the letter, if you really haven’t got it—bring it today, you must, you must.”
“Today I can’t possibly, because I’m going back to the monastery and I won’t come to see you for the next two days—three or four perhaps—because Father Zossima—”
“Four days, what nonsense! Listen. Did you laugh at me very much?”
“I didn’t laugh at all.”
“Why not?”
“Because I believed everything you said.”
“You’re insulting me!”

“Not at all. As soon as I read it, I thought that all of it would come true, because as soon as Father Zossima dies, I am to leave the monastery. Then I’ll go back and finish my studies, and when you reach the legal age we will be married. I will love you. I haven’t had time to think about it, but I believe I couldn’t find a better wife than you, and Father Zossima tells me I must marry.”
“But I’m a cripple, wheeled about in a chair,” laughed Lise, blushing crimson.
“I’ll wheel you about myself, but I’m sure you’ll be well by then.”

“But you’re mad,” said Lise, nervously, “to make all this nonsense out of a joke! Here’s mamma, perhaps very _à propos_. Mamma, how slow you always are, how can you take so long! And here’s Yulia with the ice!”

“Oh, Lise, don’t scream, above all don’t scream. That scream drives me ... How can I help it when you put the lint in a different place? I’ve been hunting and hunting—I do believe you did it on purpose.”
“But I couldn’t know he would come with a bad finger, or else perhaps I would have done it on purpose. My darling mamma, you’re starting to say really witty things.”

“Never mind my being witty, but I must say you show a fine feeling for Alexey Fyodorovitch’s suffering! Oh, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, what’s killing me isn’t any one thing in particular, not Herzenstube, but everything together, that’s what is too much for me.”

“That’s enough, mamma, enough about Herzenstube,” Lise laughed gaily. “Hurry with the lint and the lotion, mamma. That’s just Goulard’s water, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I remember the name now, but it’s a splendid lotion. Would you believe it, mamma, on the way here he got into a fight with the boys in the street, and a boy bit his finger. Isn’t he a child, a child himself? Is he fit to be married after that? Because just imagine, he wants to be married, mamma. Just think of him married, wouldn’t it be funny, wouldn’t it be awful?”
And Lise kept laughing her thin, hysterical giggle, looking slyly at Alyosha.
“But why married, Lise? What makes you talk of such a thing? It’s quite out of place—and perhaps the boy was rabid.”
“Why, mamma! As though there were rabid boys!”

“Why not, Lise, as though I had said something stupid! Your boy might have been bitten by a mad dog and he would go mad and bite anyone near him. How well she has bandaged it, Alexey Fyodorovitch! I couldn’t have done it. Do you still feel the pain?”
“It’s nothing much now.”
“You’re not afraid of water?” asked Lise.

“Come, that’s enough, Lise, perhaps I really was a bit too quick to talk about the boy being rabid, and you pounced on it at once. Katerina Ivanovna has only just heard that you’re here, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she simply rushed at me, she’s dying to see you, dying!”
“Ach, mamma, go to them yourself. He can’t go just now, he’s in too much pain.”
“Not at all, I can go quite well,” said Alyosha.
“What! You’re going away? Is that what you’re saying?”

“Well, when I’ve seen them, I’ll come back here and we can talk as much as you like. But I’d like to see Katerina Ivanovna right away, because I’m very anxious to be back at the monastery as soon as I can.”
“Mamma, take him away quickly. Alexey Fyodorovitch, don’t bother to come and see me afterwards, just go straight back to your monastery, and good riddance. I want to sleep, I didn’t sleep all night.”
“Ah, Lise, you’re only joking, but how I wish you would sleep!” cried Madame Hohlakov.
“I don’t know what I’ve done.... I’ll stay another three minutes, five if you like,” muttered Alyosha.
“Even five! Do take him away quickly, mamma, he’s a monster.”

“Lise, you’re crazy. Let’s go, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she’s too capricious today. I’m afraid to cross her. Oh, the trouble one has with nervous girls! Perhaps she really will be able to sleep after seeing you. How quickly you’ve made her sleepy, and how fortunate that is!”
“Ah, mamma, how sweetly you talk! I must kiss you for it, mamma.”

“And I kiss you too, Lise. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov began mysteriously and importantly, speaking in a rapid whisper. “I don’t want to suggest anything, I don’t want to lift the veil, you will see for yourself what’s going on. It’s appalling. It’s the most fantastic farce. She loves your brother Ivan, and she is doing her utmost to persuade herself that she loves your brother Dmitri. It’s appalling! I’ll go in with you, and if they don’t throw me out, I’ll stay to the end.”
